summary:
Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is a first-person 3D story game that runs in a web browser, made for school-age space enthusiasts. A fictional comet is heading for Earth, and the knowledge needed to stop it lies in six real machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 12 science station, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity.

In each chapter the player scans the machine, reads fact cards that name their NASA sources, operates it in a short simulation, and then chooses whether to take a piece or leave the site untouched. Along the way players learn each mission's objectives, what it achieved, and how it shaped the missions that followed. What the player learns decides the ending. A map shows 21 real objects left on other worlds.

The challenge asks for a story that teaches what this equipment is and why it matters. Our game shows that abandoned hardware still holds knowledge, and asks players to weigh science against preserving history.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is a first-person 3D story game that runs in a web browser. A fictional comet, KAIROS, is heading for Earth. In the prologue Commander Mitra fails, again, to push it aside in simulation. So she and her robot partner Evvi visit six real machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars: Surveyor 3 and the Apollo 12 landing site, the Apollo 12 science station, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity.

Each chapter follows the same steps. The player walks to the machine, scans its parts to open fact cards, watches a reconstruction of what happened there, tries something hands-on (re-enacting how Apollo 12 cut the camera from Surveyor 3, driving a rover, flying a helicopter, reading a seismometer trace), and then makes one choice: take a piece for the mission, or leave the historic site untouched. Each chapter earns a data card, and the cards decide how the Finale goes. If a chapter is skipped, the mission has to guess at that part.

READ MODE

The same six missions can be read instead of played. Read mode is a stamp book: each mission is a short deck of seven cards (a picture, the question the mission was sent to answer, one number to remember, what it achieved, a closer look at its parts, three things to learn, and a question). Answering the question earns that mission's stamp. It is built from the same sourced fact cards as the game, so the two cannot disagree. It is there for anyone who prefers to read, for classrooms, and for devices that cannot run the 3D game.

THE ARTIFACT MAP

A map shows 21 real objects NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, each with what it is, why it was sent, what it found and a link to the NASA page.

BENEFITS

Players learn why each mission was sent, what it achieved and how it helped the missions that followed. Every fact card names the NASA page or report it came from. The game is free, runs in a browser with nothing to install, works with keyboard and mouse or touch, and has settings for text size, sound, graphics level and whether dialogue moves on by itself.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want school-age space enthusiasts to see abandoned hardware as knowledge that is still useful, and to think about a real question: when is it right to disturb a historic site for science? The game lets the player decide, records the choice, and keeps a count of sites left undisturbed.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React, Three.js with React Three Fiber and drei, Zustand, Vite, Vitest and Playwright for testing, and Cloudflare Workers for hosting. The Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, Apollo Lunar Module and astronaut models and the Moon, Mars and Earth maps are NASA media. Surveyor 3, the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the science station are rebuilt by hand from NASA descriptions. Evvi's body is a free (CC0) robot model by Quaternius. The text is set in IBM Plex. Music and sound effects are generated in the browser. No special hardware was used.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The story turns the challenge's subject into the solution: the old machines are what save Earth. The Apollo 12 crew really did walk to Surveyor 3 and cut parts off it, and the game asks the player to face the same decision. Reconstructions are drawn as cyan projections, so the player can always tell a rebuilt moment from the real machine in front of them.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: the game states what is real and what is fiction, and labels every simulation and reconstruction.

Audience: plain language and short lines for young players.

Access: a read mode, touch controls, adjustable text and a low-graphics setting.

Respect for the sites: the choice to leave things untouched is always available and always recorded.
